topic.subject: science
topic.title: Sorting materials into groups
topic.scope: properties of materials, lustre, hardness, solubility, floating and sinking, transparency

misconceptions.statement: A chair is a material, not an object.
misconceptions.why: Students often use the name of the object and the material interchangeably in daily speech.
misconceptions.fix: An object is the thing itself (like a chair), while the material is what it is made of (like wood or plastic).

probe.question: If a spoon is made of steel, which one is the material?

misconceptions.root_belief: an object and its substance are the same thing

misconceptions.why: Metals are the most common examples of lustrous materials shown in textbooks.
misconceptions.fix: While most metals have lustre, some non-metals like diamond or polished granite also show shine.

probe.question: Is a polished diamond a metal because it shines?

misconceptions.statement: Hard materials cannot be broken easily.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse scientific hardness (resistance to scratching) with strength or toughness.
misconceptions.fix: Hardness refers to how difficult it is to scratch a material; a glass sheet is hard but breaks easily.

probe.question: Is glass a soft material because it breaks when dropped?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Sugar disappears completely when it dissolves in water.
misconceptions.why: Since the sugar is no longer visible, students think it has ceased to exist.
misconceptions.fix: Sugar breaks into tiny particles that are too small to see, but they are still present in the water.

probe.question: If you dissolve sugar in water, why does the water taste sweet?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the sugar turned into water

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: Dissolving is the same thing as melting.
misconceptions.why: In both processes, a solid seems to turn into a liquid state.
misconceptions.fix: Melting requires heat to change state, while dissolving involves a substance mixing into a solvent.

probe.question: When you put salt in water, is the salt melting?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar visual outcomes imply same process

misconceptions.why: Students usually only see solids like salt or sugar dissolving.
misconceptions.fix: Some gases, like oxygen and carbon dioxide, can dissolve in water and are vital for aquatic life.

probe.question: How do fish breathe underwater if there is no air in the water?

misconceptions.root_belief: matter in different states cannot mix

misconceptions.statement: Heavy objects always sink and light objects always float.
misconceptions.why: Students observe heavy stones sinking and light feathers floating, ignoring the role of material type.
misconceptions.fix: Floating depends on the material's density relative to water, not just its total weight.

probe.question: Will a tiny iron nail float because it is very light?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: A large piece of wood will sink while a small chip of wood will float.
misconceptions.why: Students believe that increasing the amount of a material changes its ability to float.
misconceptions.fix: If a material floats, any size of that same material will float because the property remains the same.

probe.question: If a small wooden stick floats, what will a huge wooden log do?

misconceptions.root_belief: properties change with the amount of substance

misconceptions.statement: Transparent objects like glass do not block any light at all.
misconceptions.why: Because we can see through them clearly, students assume light passes through 100% unaffected.
misconceptions.fix: Even transparent objects reflect or absorb a tiny amount of light, which is why we can still see the glass itself.

probe.question: If glass blocked no light, would you be able to see the glass surface?

misconceptions.statement: Opaque objects are always dark in color.
misconceptions.why: Students associate 'opaque' with shadows and lack of light, leading to a color bias.
misconceptions.fix: Opaque simply means light cannot pass through; a bright white wall or a yellow book is opaque.

probe.question: Is a bright white plastic sheet opaque or transparent?

misconceptions.statement: All liquids mix with each other because they are all fluids.
misconceptions.why: Students observe water and milk mixing easily and generalize this to all liquids.
misconceptions.fix: Some liquids, like oil and water, do not mix and are called immiscible.

probe.question: What happens when you stir mustard oil into a glass of water?

misconceptions.root_belief: things in the same state must behave identically

misconceptions.statement: Lustre is a coating applied to the surface of an object.
misconceptions.why: Students are familiar with paint or polish making things look shiny.
misconceptions.fix: Lustre is an inherent property of the material itself, often seen when it is freshly cut.

probe.question: If you cut a shiny metal rod in half, will the inside surface be shiny?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only the outside is shiny
